explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Moses says the fruit of your womb will be cursed, "as well as the produce of your land, the calves of your herds, and the lambs of your flocks" (Deuteronomy 28:18). Family, farm and pasture all land in one verse. I think Moses wants nobody walking away believing their own corner of life is exempt.

Not quite, friend. Moses says, "The fruit of your womb will be cursed, as well as the produce of your land, the calves of your herds, and the lambs of your flocks" (Deuteronomy 28:18). So the curse reaches the children, the crops and the animals too. The whole household is on that list.

explanations.answer: Everything they put their hand to
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Moses says confusion and reproof will land "in all to which you put your hand" (Deuteronomy 28:20). You know those mornings when the phone, the car and the printer all give up before you've had a chance? Now picture that following you everywhere.

explanations.answer: Their fields but not their homes
explanations.explanation: Close, but Moses doesn't split it like that. He says the confusion and reproof come "in all to which you put your hand" (Deuteronomy 28:20). He even names the basket and the kneading bowl earlier in the same list (Deuteronomy 28:17).

explanations.answer: Their homes but not their fields
explanations.explanation: That cuts it in half, and Moses doesn't. The verse says "in all to which you put your hand" (Deuteronomy 28:20). He has already said they will be cursed "in the city and cursed in the country" (Deuteronomy 28:16), so the fields are in it, and so is everywhere else.

Yes, forsaking. The verse says the curses come "because of the wickedness you have committed in forsaking Him" (Deuteronomy 28:20). Forsaking means leaving Him behind, and that's the word Moses picks. He says it plainly right there in the verse.

Fearing is a fair guess, but it isn't the word in the verse. Moses says the wickedness was "in forsaking Him" (Deuteronomy 28:20). Later he says they need to be careful to observe the law "that you may fear this glorious and awesome name" (Deuteronomy 28:58), so fearing is what he's calling them toward.

Thanking sounds sweet, but the verse says something else. The wickedness Moses names is "in forsaking Him" (Deuteronomy 28:20). Later he does say they "did not serve the LORD your God with joy and gladness of heart" (Deuteronomy 28:47), but the word in this verse is forsaking.

Dust and powder is right. Moses says the LORD will turn "the rain of your land into dust and powder" (Deuteronomy 28:24). Rain that shows up as dust, under a sky he has already called bronze (Deuteronomy 28:23). Imagine checking the forecast and seeing nothing but dust.

Hail and ice aren't in the verse. Moses says the LORD will turn "the rain of your land into dust and powder" (Deuteronomy 28:24). That comes right after he says, "The sky over your head will be bronze, and the earth beneath you iron" (Deuteronomy 28:23).

Fire and smoke is a dramatic guess, but it isn't what Moses says. The verse says the LORD will turn "the rain of your land into dust and powder" (Deuteronomy 28:24). It descends from the sky until they are destroyed, and dust is the word he uses.

That one's flipped around, friend. Israel is the one on the run. Moses says, "You will march out against them in one direction but flee from them in seven" (Deuteronomy 28:25). The statement had the enemies doing the fleeing.

Yes, it's the other way around. Moses says, "You will march out against them in one direction but flee from them in seven" (Deuteronomy 28:25). Israel is the one scattering, not the enemies. The same verse opens by saying the LORD will cause them to be defeated before their enemies.

An object of horror is right. Moses says, "You will be an object of horror to all the kingdoms of the earth" (Deuteronomy 28:25). That's how every kingdom will see them. I think it's a hard thing to hear right after the blessings he listed first (Deuteronomy 28:1-14).

Feared sounds strong, but it isn't what Moses says. He says, "You will be an object of horror to all the kingdoms of the earth" (Deuteronomy 28:25). The word is horror, and it comes right after the defeat he describes in the same verse.

Pity is a gentler word than the one Moses uses. He says, "You will be an object of horror to all the kingdoms of the earth" (Deuteronomy 28:25). The kingdoms of the earth see horror, and that's the word on the page.

Moses says it the other way, friend. Day after day Israel will be oppressed and plundered, "with no one to save you" (Deuteronomy 28:29). No rescuer shows up in that verse. I think this is a heavy line, so I'll let it sit.

Yes, no one comes. Moses says Israel will be oppressed and plundered day after day, "with no one to save you" (Deuteronomy 28:29). The verse names no rescuer at all. This is one of the heavy lines in the passage.

explanations.answer: He will not live in it
explanations.explanation: That's it. Moses says, "You will build a house but will not live in it" (Deuteronomy 28:30). It's like finishing a whole project at work and watching someone else get the credit. He lists it right beside the vineyard whose fruit they won't enjoy (Deuteronomy 28:30).

explanations.answer: It will burn to the ground
explanations.explanation: Fire is a dramatic guess, but there's no fire in the verse. Moses says, "You will build a house but will not live in it" (Deuteronomy 28:30). The house gets built, and the builder doesn't live in it.

explanations.answer: It will fall in a storm
explanations.explanation: A storm isn't in the verse. Moses says, "You will build a house but will not live in it" (Deuteronomy 28:30). He doesn't say how it happens, only that the one who built it won't live there.

It's the opposite, friend. Moses says, "You will plant a vineyard but will not enjoy its fruit" (Deuteronomy 28:30). The planting is theirs, and the enjoying isn't. It sits right after the house they won't live in (Deuteronomy 28:30).

Yes, false. Moses says, "You will plant a vineyard but will not enjoy its fruit" (Deuteronomy 28:30). All that work in the soil, and no enjoying what grows. It comes right after the house they build but won't live in.

Yes, Moses says it plainly. "Your sons and daughters will be given to another nation, while your eyes grow weary looking for them day after day, with no power in your hand" (Deuteronomy 28:32). I think this one hurts. Let's let it sit for a second.

This one is true, friend, and it's a hard one. Moses says, "Your sons and daughters will be given to another nation, while your eyes grow weary looking for them day after day, with no power in your hand" (Deuteronomy 28:32). I think this line hurts. Nothing to add to it.

Gods of wood and stone is right. Moses says that in a nation neither they nor their fathers have known, "there you will worship other gods", and he names them as gods of wood and stone (Deuteronomy 28:36). Even the king they appoint is brought there too, because the LORD will bring them both (Deuteronomy 28:36). That's a long way from home.

Sun and moon is a good guess, but they aren't in this verse. Moses says they will worship other gods there, "gods of wood and stone" (Deuteronomy 28:36). It's in a nation neither they nor their fathers have known.

explanations.answer: The LORD in a new temple
explanations.explanation: A new temple for the LORD isn't what Moses describes. He says that in that unknown nation "there you will worship other gods", and he names them as gods of wood and stone (Deuteronomy 28:36). The verse points away from the LORD, not toward a new place to worship Him.

Locusts it is. Moses says they will sow much seed but harvest little, "because the locusts will consume it" (Deuteronomy 28:38). He brings them back a few verses later: "Swarms of locusts will consume all your trees and the produce of your land" (Deuteronomy 28:42). Plant a lot, pull in a little, and every locust gets a seat at the table.

Frogs are a fun guess, but they aren't in this verse. Moses says the seed is eaten "because the locusts will consume it" (Deuteronomy 28:38). He names locusts again in Deuteronomy 28:42, with swarms that consume all the trees and the produce of the land.

Gnats are a small guess for a big problem, and they aren't in this verse. Moses says they will harvest little "because the locusts will consume it" (Deuteronomy 28:38). Locusts come up again in Deuteronomy 28:42, as swarms that consume the trees and the land's produce.

explanations.answer: He will rise higher and become the head
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. Moses says, "The foreigner living among you will rise higher and higher above you, while you sink down lower and lower" (Deuteronomy 28:43). Then he adds, "He will be the head, and you will be the tail" (Deuteronomy 28:44). He also says the foreigner will lend to them while they will not lend to him (Deuteronomy 28:44).

explanations.answer: He will leave the land for good
explanations.explanation: Leaving isn't in the verse. Moses says, "The foreigner living among you will rise higher and higher above you, while you sink down lower and lower" (Deuteronomy 28:43). In the next verse he says, "He will be the head, and you will be the tail" (Deuteronomy 28:44). The foreigner is the one going up.

That's flipped around from what Moses says. He says the foreigner "will rise higher and higher above you, while you sink down lower and lower" (Deuteronomy 28:43). Then, "He will be the head, and you will be the tail" (Deuteronomy 28:44). Israel is the one sinking, not the foreigner.

explanations.answer: Serve the LORD with joy and gladness
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's the reason Moses gives. He says, "Because you did not serve the LORD your God with joy and gladness of heart in all your abundance" (Deuteronomy 28:47). The phrase "in all your abundance" is the part that gets me.

explanations.answer: Share their riches with the poor
explanations.explanation: Sharing is a good thing to do, but it isn't what this verse says. Moses says they "did not serve the LORD your God with joy and gladness of heart in all your abundance" (Deuteronomy 28:47). The reason he gives is about serving the LORD with joy and gladness.

explanations.answer: Build a great temple for the LORD
explanations.explanation: A temple isn't mentioned in this verse. Moses says, "Because you did not serve the LORD your God with joy and gladness of heart in all your abundance" (Deuteronomy 28:47). The reason on the page is joy and gladness in serving Him.

Enemies is right. Moses says, "you will serve your enemies the LORD will send against you in famine, thirst, nakedness, and destitution" (Deuteronomy 28:48). Famine, thirst, nakedness and destitution come along with it. The next line puts an iron yoke on their neck (Deuteronomy 28:48).

Neighbors sounds gentler, but that isn't the word. Moses says, "you will serve your enemies the LORD will send against you in famine, thirst, nakedness, and destitution" (Deuteronomy 28:48). They are enemies, and the LORD is the one who sends them.

Priests aren't in this verse. Moses says, "you will serve your enemies the LORD will send against you in famine, thirst, nakedness, and destitution" (Deuteronomy 28:48). The ones they serve are enemies, and the hardship comes with it.

The language is part of the problem, friend. Moses calls it "a nation whose language you will not understand" (Deuteronomy 28:49). It swoops down "like an eagle" (Deuteronomy 28:49). They won't understand a word of it.

Yes, they won't understand it. Moses says the LORD will bring "a nation whose language you will not understand" (Deuteronomy 28:49). That nation comes from far away, from the ends of the earth, and swoops down like an eagle. Not understanding the language is part of the picture.

explanations.answer: No respect for the old and no pity for the young
explanations.explanation: That's the whole line. Moses calls it "a ruthless nation with no respect for the old and no pity for the young" (Deuteronomy 28:50). Neither end of the age range gets a break. I think that's why he reaches for the word ruthless.

explanations.answer: Respect for the old but no pity for the young
explanations.explanation: That splits it, and Moses doesn't. He says it's "a ruthless nation with no respect for the old and no pity for the young" (Deuteronomy 28:50). The old get no respect from them either. Neither group gets a break.

explanations.answer: Pity for the young but no respect for the old
explanations.explanation: That gives the young a break, and Moses doesn't. He says it's "a ruthless nation with no respect for the old and no pity for the young" (Deuteronomy 28:50). There's no pity for the young in that verse. Neither end of the age range is spared.

explanations.answer: The high fortified walls they trust in
explanations.explanation: The walls are right. Moses says the siege goes on "until the high and fortified walls in which you trust have fallen" (Deuteronomy 28:52). Those are the walls Israel trusts in, and the verse says they come down. It happens in all their cities, throughout the land the LORD gave them (Deuteronomy 28:52).

explanations.answer: The tents of their camp in the field
explanations.explanation: Tents aren't in this verse. Moses says the siege lasts "until the high and fortified walls in which you trust have fallen" (Deuteronomy 28:52). The enemy besieges their cities, and the walls are what finally fall.

explanations.answer: The storehouses they built for grain
explanations.explanation: Storehouses aren't mentioned in this verse. Moses says the siege goes on "until the high and fortified walls in which you trust have fallen" (Deuteronomy 28:52). He does say in the verse before that the enemy will leave them no grain, new wine or oil (Deuteronomy 28:51).

Yes, Moses says it. "The most gentle and refined man among you will begrudge his brother, the wife he embraces, and the rest of his children who have survived" (Deuteronomy 28:54). He says it happens in the siege and distress the enemy inflicts (Deuteronomy 28:55). This part is heavy, so I'll say it plainly and leave it there.

This one is true, friend, and it's heavy. Moses says that even the most gentle and refined man among them will begrudge his brother, his wife and his surviving children (Deuteronomy 28:54). He will refuse to share with any of them, because he has nothing left in the siege and distress that the enemy inflicts (Deuteronomy 28:55). I think this part hurts.

Yes, Egypt comes back. Moses says, "He will afflict you again with all the diseases you dreaded in Egypt, and they will cling to you" (Deuteronomy 28:60). Back in verse 27 he named "the boils of Egypt" too (Deuteronomy 28:27). Egypt keeps showing up in this list.

It's true, friend. Moses says, "He will afflict you again with all the diseases you dreaded in Egypt, and they will cling to you" (Deuteronomy 28:60). The diseases they dreaded in Egypt are on the list. He also named "the boils of Egypt" earlier (Deuteronomy 28:27).

Moses goes past the page, friend. He says, "The LORD will also bring upon you every sickness and plague not recorded in this Book of the Law, until you are destroyed" (Deuteronomy 28:61). So the sicknesses written in the book aren't the whole list. It's a hard one to hear.

Yes, false. Moses says, "The LORD will also bring upon you every sickness and plague not recorded in this Book of the Law, until you are destroyed" (Deuteronomy 28:61). So the list reaches past what's written in the book. The sicknesses don't stop where the page does.

Few is right. Moses says, "You who were as numerous as the stars in the sky will be left few in number, because you would not obey the voice of the LORD your God" (Deuteronomy 28:62). From as numerous as the stars to few in number is a long drop. A sky full of stars is a lot of people to come down from.

Many is where they started, not where Moses says they end up. He says, "You who were as numerous as the stars in the sky will be left few in number" (Deuteronomy 28:62). The curse turns the stars into few.

Strong isn't the word in the verse. Moses says, "You who were as numerous as the stars in the sky will be left few in number" (Deuteronomy 28:62). He's talking about how many they are, not how strong.

Among all the nations is right. Moses says, "Then the LORD will scatter you among all the nations, from one end of the earth to the other" (Deuteronomy 28:64). The uprooting comes first (Deuteronomy 28:63), then the scattering. And there, he says, they will worship other gods, gods of wood and stone, which neither they nor their fathers have known.

The wilderness of Zin isn't mentioned here. Moses says, "Then the LORD will scatter you among all the nations, from one end of the earth to the other" (Deuteronomy 28:64). That's much farther than one wilderness. The scattering reaches one end of the earth to the other.

Gilead isn't in this verse. Moses says, "Then the LORD will scatter you among all the nations, from one end of the earth to the other" (Deuteronomy 28:64). It's the nations, not one place across the river. The scattering reaches from one end of the earth to the other.

Dread is right. Moses says, "because of the dread in your hearts of the terrifying sights you will see" (Deuteronomy 28:67). Just before it he says, "you will be afraid night and day, never certain of survival" (Deuteronomy 28:66). I think this is one of the heaviest stretches of the whole speech.

Pride isn't what Moses names. He says, "because of the dread in your hearts of the terrifying sights you will see" (Deuteronomy 28:67). The feeling in their hearts is dread. A verse earlier he says they will be afraid night and day (Deuteronomy 28:66).

Greed isn't in the verse. Moses says, "because of the dread in your hearts of the terrifying sights you will see" (Deuteronomy 28:67). It's dread that fills their hearts. The verse before says, "you will be afraid night and day" (Deuteronomy 28:66).

That's what the text says. Moses says, "There you will sell yourselves to your enemies as male and female slaves, but no one will buy you" (Deuteronomy 28:68). I think this is the hardest picture of all, a people who offer themselves and still find no taker. It's the last line of this passage.

explanations.answer: Their enemies will buy them all
explanations.explanation: That's not what Moses says. He says, "There you will sell yourselves to your enemies as male and female slaves, but no one will buy you" (Deuteronomy 28:68). They offer themselves, and no one buys. It's a heavy way for the passage to end.

Pharaoh isn't in the verse, and neither is a release. Moses says, "There you will sell yourselves to your enemies as male and female slaves, but no one will buy you" (Deuteronomy 28:68). He also says the LORD will return them to Egypt in ships, by a route he said they should never see again. It's a hard line, and it's where this passage closes.
